specPoints.text: know that fusion is the energy source for stars
explain why nuclear fusion does not happen at low temperatures and pressures, due to electrostatic repulsion of protons

primer.text: Stars are hydrogen furnaces: in their cores deuterium and tritium fuse into helium, and the outward pressure of that released heat holds the star up against gravity. Getting two nuclei to fuse means beating electrostatic repulsion — so millions of degrees and crushing pressures are the entry price, found naturally only in star cores.

lessons.title: Fusion in stars
sourceHeadings: Forces acting on a stable star
lessons.opening: A star is a huge ball of mostly hydrogen, and in its core hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium — deuterium plus tritium can yield helium-4 and a neutron. Fusion is the energy source for stars, and its heat supplies an outward pressure that stops the star collapsing under its own gravity.
keyPoints: Stars are mostly hydrogen, and core fusion turns hydrogen into helium.
A deuterium nucleus plus a tritium nucleus can fuse into helium-4 and a neutron.
Fusion is the energy source that keeps stars shining.
Outward pressure from fusion heat balances gravity's inward pull in a stable star.
In larger, hotter stars helium can fuse into heavier elements.

low.restatement: Star fuel = hydrogen; star support = fusion pressure against gravity.
low.analogy: A jet of water from a fountain holding a ball aloft: the spray (fusion pressure) balances the ball's weight (gravity).
low.examPointer: Equilibrium wording earns marks: outward pressure versus inward gravity, not just 'gravity pulls'.

medium.restatement: The D–T reaction ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n carries 5 mass units and 2 charge units through unchanged — conservation in action.
medium.analogy: A balanced see-saw: whatever mass sits on one side (the fuel nuclei) must reappear on the other (the products).
medium.examPointer: Balance-check questions are free marks: add top numbers, add bottom numbers, state both equalities.

check.stem: What gas are stars mostly made of?

options.explanation: Hydrogen is the main stellar gas and the fusion fuel.
Helium is the product of fusion, not the main fuel.
Carbon appears in later fusion stages of larger stars only.
Oxygen is not a stellar fuel at this level.

check.stem: Deuterium plus tritium fuse to give…

options.explanation: Mass 2 + 3 → 4 + 1; charge 1 + 1 → 2.
A neutron is also released.
The helium nucleus is the main product.
That is a different fusion route from the corpus example.

check.stem: What stops a stable star from collapsing?

options.text: fusion heat supplies outward pressure that balances gravity
options.explanation: Inward gravity and outward fusion pressure hold equilibrium.
Magnetism is not the balancing force here.
The wind is an outflow, not the support pressure.
Stars have no solid surface.

check.stem: Why is stellar fusion important for life on Earth?

options.text: the Sun's fusion output supplies the energy Earth depends on
options.explanation: Solar fusion is the origin of the energy that sustains life.
Fossil fuels store ancient sunlight, not fresh fusion.
Oxygen comes from photosynthesis, not fusion.
Blocking radiation is not what fusion does.

check.stem: In larger stars where the core runs hot enough, helium nuclei can…

options.explanation: Hotter cores extend fusion beyond hydrogen.
Helium does not decay to hydrogen here.

options.text: only be made by fission of iron
options.explanation: Fission of iron is not a stellar process at this level.
Surface evaporation is unrelated to core fusion.

check.stem: State the energy source of stars.
check.modelAnswer: Nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium in the star's core.

check.stem: State the outcome of the deuterium–tritium fusion reaction.
check.modelAnswer: Deuterium and tritium fuse into a helium-4 nucleus plus one neutron.

check.stem: Explain why a stable star does not simply shrink under its own gravity.
check.modelAnswer: Gravity pulls the star's material inward, but fusion in the core releases heat that raises the pressure outward; the two balance, so the star stays stable instead of collapsing.

check.stem: Check the balance of the D–T reaction: mass numbers 2 + 3 on the left against helium-4 plus a neutron on the right, and atomic numbers 1 + 1 against 2.
check.modelAnswer: Mass: 2 + 3 = 5 and 4 + 1 = 5, so mass balances. Atomic: 1 + 1 = 2 and the helium side is 2, so charge balances too.

lessons.title: The conditions for fusion
lessons.opening: Two protons both carry positive charge, so they repel each other electrostatically — fusion only happens when nuclei slam together hard enough to beat that repulsion. That takes extremely high temperatures, so nuclei move very fast, and extremely high pressures, so they are squeezed close enough to collide; naturally, only star cores reach the millions of degrees required.
keyPoints: Protons are positively charged, so they repel each other electrostatically.
Fusion needs nuclei moving fast enough to beat the repulsion and get extremely close.
Extremely high temperatures supply the kinetic energy; extremely high pressures squeeze nuclei together.
Millions of degrees are needed — found naturally only in star cores.
Higher temperature means faster nuclei and closer approaches; higher pressure means more collisions.

low.restatement: Hot and squeezed: speed beats repulsion, crowding supplies the collisions.
low.analogy: Two magnets with like poles facing: you must shove them hard and fast to touch — gentle approaches always slide apart.
low.examPointer: Always tie the barrier (electrostatic repulsion of protons) to the cure (high temperature and pressure) — one without the other drops marks.

medium.restatement: Kinetic energy scales with temperature, so hotter nuclei approach closer against Coulomb repulsion; pressure raises collision frequency.
medium.analogy: Stadium crowd dynamics: only sprinting fans reach the middle of the pitch, and a fuller stadium means more of them try every second.
medium.examPointer: The exam answer must name the repulsion of protons as the reason, not just 'it is too cold'.

check.stem: Why do two protons resist fusing?

options.text: their positive charges repel each other electrostatically
options.explanation: Like charges repel — that is the barrier fusion must beat.

options.text: because they are too heavy to move
options.explanation: Proton mass is not the barrier.
Gravity pulls masses together, not apart.
Protons are positively charged.

check.stem: What allows two nuclei to overcome the repulsion and fuse?

options.text: very high kinetic energy from extreme temperatures
options.explanation: Fast, hot nuclei push through the electrostatic barrier.
Cooler nuclei move slower and fuse less.
Electrons cannot neutralise nuclear repulsion here.
Shielding absorbs radiation; it does not fuse nuclei.

check.stem: Where are fusion conditions found naturally?

options.explanation: Only stellar cores reach the millions of degrees needed.
The mantle is far too cool.
Lightning is hot but nowhere near hot enough.
Boiler temperatures are thousands of degrees short.

check.stem: Raising the pressure helps fusion because…

options.text: nuclei are squeezed into a smaller space and collide more often
options.explanation: More collisions per second means more chances to fuse.
Pressure does not slow nuclei; temperature does the speeding.
Repulsion remains; collisions simply get closer and more frequent.
Mass is unchanged by pressure.

check.stem: The temperature needed for hydrogen fusion is about…

options.explanation: Star-core temperatures run into millions of degrees.
Nine orders of magnitude too cool.
Still millions short of the requirement.
Fusion cannot run anywhere near everyday temperatures.

check.stem: State the two conditions required for nuclear fusion.
check.modelAnswer: Extremely high temperatures and extremely high pressures.

check.stem: State why protons repel each other.
check.modelAnswer: Protons carry positive charges, and like charges repel electrostatically.

check.stem: Explain why fusion cannot run at low temperatures or pressures.
check.modelAnswer: At low temperature nuclei move slowly and cannot push through the electrostatic repulsion of their positive charges; at low pressure they rarely meet closely enough, so collisions that end in fusion are vanishingly rare.

check.stem: A proposal claims hydrogen fusion could run at 5,000 °C in a laboratory flask. Judge the claim.
check.modelAnswer: Hydrogen fusion needs temperatures of millions of degrees so protons can overcome their repulsion; 5,000 °C is millions short, so the flask cannot sustain fusion.

glossary.definition: The mutual repulsion of positively charged protons that fusion must overcome.
The hydrogen isotope with one proton and one neutron; a stellar fusion fuel.
The heavier hydrogen isotope that fuses with deuterium into helium-4 plus a neutron.

workedExample.prompt: Why is hydrogen fusion not currently possible on Earth?
steps: Hydrogen nuclei carry positive charges, so two of them repel each other.
Overcoming that repulsion needs very high temperatures to give the nuclei enough energy.
The product shown, helium, is inert and not radioactive — waste is not the obstacle.
Hydrogen is abundant, and the energy output would be huge — supply and payoff are not the obstacles.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Hydrogen nuclei require very high temperatures to fuse together, which is why hydrogen fusion is not currently possible on Earth.
